value: to do something to the horse himself
note: Two needs, each with a reason in the story. First, the horse must be out of the stable: 'So spirited a creature would have certainly roused the soundest of sleepers… It was absolutely necessary to do it in the open air' (¶223). Second, practice first: 'so astute a man as Straker would not undertake this delicate tendon-nicking without a little practice' (¶228).

Inside first. Needed so that lead_out's '{guard: $via}' finds the guard of the stables (Hunter), and so that 'through stable_door' means out on the moor.

set.value: lad on guard in the stables for the night

note: The guard must sit on a role fact for lead_out's guard rule to apply. The drugging effect (Hunter drugged) then meets that need of leading the horse out, which serves Straker's aim.

why: Once the patches above are in, the reader links the drugging through a chain. The drug's effect (Hunter drugged) meets lead_out's guard need, Hunter being guard of the stables inside the stable door. Leading the horse out in turn meets the nick's need that the horse be outside the stable. The drugging therefore serves the aim to lame the horse through the linked lead_out step, not directly. Holmes's words: 'why should he drug his own stable-boy?' (¶220).

The question asks why an unknown person led the horse out, so its entry has no agent to presuppose an action of. The reader gets there through Straker's aim. With q.who_took circled as straker, his leading-out is linked to his intention in q.straker_reason or q.knife, which is to lame the horse with the nick. That link fits because the nick needs the horse outside the stable door. The story gives that need: 'So spirited a creature would have certainly roused the soundest of sleepers… It was absolutely necessary to do it in the open air' (¶223). That linked need is exactly this question's answer.

The question asks who made away with the favourite and why, so its entry has no agent. The reader reaches the answer through other questions. They circle q.who_took=straker and link his leading-out to the laming aim of q.straker_reason, using the nick's need that the horse be out of the stable (¶223). Separately, the horse's tracks show it went off alone from the hollow (¶120: 'The horse was alone before'). Together these give 'led out to be harmed and got loose'. The story then states it at ¶223 and ¶231 ('it bolted').

The reader names who led the horse out by inference from what is told, not by linking an aim to it. The stable dog was set on the stranger that evening, yet it made no noise when the horse was taken (¶29, ¶34, ¶181–182), so the man who came at night was someone it knew well. The door was locked after the stranger left and found open at seven (¶31, ¶33), and the master of the stable keeps a key. Straker set out alone for the stables at one (¶32) and died beside the horse in the hollow (¶35, ¶37). Holmes draws the same conclusion: 'Obviously the midnight visitor was some one whom the dog knew well' (¶219). Straker's motive for the leading-out (to lame the horse in the open air, ¶223) comes afterwards and explains the act; it is not how the reader picks out its agent.
